The words

In thine own ways, O God of love,
We wait the visits of thy grace,
Our souls desire is to thy Name,
And the remembrance of thy face.

My thoughts are searching, Lord, for thee,
'Mongst the black shades of lonesome night;
My earnest cries salute the skies
Before the dawn restore the light.

Look, how rebellious men deride
The tender patience of my God;
But they shall see thy lifted hand,
And feel the scourges of thy rod.

Hark, the Eternal rends the sky,
A mighty voice before him goes,
A voice of music to his friends,
But threatening thunder to his foes.

Come, children, to your Father's arms,
Hide in the chambers of my grace,
Till the fierce storms be overblown,
And my revenging fury cease.

My sword shall boast its thousands slain,
And drink the blood of haughty kings,
While heavenly peace around my flock
Stretches its soft and shady wings.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Eb and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s (B♭), on the word “In”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Isaac Watts wrote these words for his Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707), Book I, collected from the Scriptures, hymn 30, headed “Prayer for deliverance answered, Isa. 26. 8-12 20 21”.

Watts' hymns were printed without tunes and sung to any tune of their metre, Long Metre (8.8.8.8). This page sets the words to MELCOMBE; any other Long Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words (1707): Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
  • Music (1782): Samuel Webbe (1740–1816)

Tune MELCOMBE by Samuel Webbe (1740–1816); words by Isaac Watts (1674–1748).

Sung to the same tune: At Thy Command, Our Dearest Lord, Awake, Our Souls, Away, Our Fears, Behold How Sinners Disagree, Bury'd in Shadows of the Night, Eternal Spirit! We Confess, From Heaven the Sinning Angels Fell, God of the Morning, at Whose Voice, Great God, to What a Glorious Height, How Vast the Treasure We Possess, My God, How Endless Is Thy Love, My God, Permit Me Not to Be, New Every Morning Is the Love, Now Let the Lord My Saviour Smile, Praise, Everlasting Praise Be Paid, Sing to the Lord That Built the Skies, So Let Our Lips and Lives Express, This Is the Word of Truth and Love, Thou Whom My Soul Admires Above, When the Great Builder Arch'd the Skies.

Questions about In Thine Own Ways, O God of Love

What is the doh of In Thine Own Ways, O God of Love?

In this version, in Eb major, doh is Eb. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does In Thine Own Ways, O God of Love start on?

It starts on s (B♭ in Eb major), a pickup on the word “In” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to s.

Is In Thine Own Ways, O God of Love in the public domain?

Yes. Isaac Watts died in 1748, Samuel Webbe died in 1816; the words were first published in 1707 and the music in 1782. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
